Results
Using kernel density and map overlay analyses, “commerce-tourism” spatial coupling distribu-
tion maps were combined with the commercial service POIs and tourist attraction POIs from the
17 historic and cultural areas. As shown in Figure 4, both commercial service POIs and tourist
attraction POIs exhibited three spatial forms: scattered point aggregation, block mass aggre-
gations, and cluster-typed aggregations (multiple-core group). The spatial structures formed by
the commercial service POIs and tourist attraction POIs were then divided into five types (Table
3): fully encircled clustering, semi-surrounding clustering, overlapping clustering, contiguous
clustering, and separate clustering. (1) Fully encircled clustering described a spatial structure
type where the tourist attraction POIs, illustrated by a scatter of points, were distributed among
commercial service POIs, which were visualized as block masses; that is, the tourist space had
been surrounded by developed commercial space. (2) Semi-surrounding clustering described a
spatial structure type where some of the commercial service POIs, which were arranged into
block masses, were distributed around the scattered tourist attraction POIs; some were isolated
from the tourist attraction POIs. (3) Overlapping clustering described a spatial structure type
where the tourist attraction POIs and commercial service POIs overlapped spatially; that is, the
developed spaces of commerce and tourism had blended together. (4) Separate clustering
described a spatial structure type where there was a clear trend of an independent division of
space between the tourist attraction POIs, characterized by cluster-typed aggregation, and com-
mercial service POIs, characterized by block masses. (5) Contiguous clustering described a
spatial structure type that had clusters of commercial and tourist attractions adjacent to one
another. Both presented an even spatial distribution pattern.
For discussion of spatial coupling relations, we further analyzed the spatial weight among the
various commercial service and tourist attraction POIs in the related study areas to determine
their main spatial functions. As shown in Figure 4, this analysis showed that three types of
historic and cultural areas could be identified as follows: commercial service oriented areas
(commercial service POIs dominated the spatial distribution), tourist attraction oriented areas
(tourist attraction POIs dominated the spatial distribution), and commerce–tourism complexes
(the spatial dominance of neither commercial service POIs nor tourist attraction POIs was
significant; Table 3).
We were then able to summarize the different spatial structures and internal order of the three
types of historic areas, according to the kernel density of the tourist attraction POIs and the five
types of commercial service POIs (Figure 5). Table 4 shows the main spatial functions of the
three historic areas types.

(1) Concerning differences between the contrasting spatial patterns of commercial services
and tourist attractions.
The spatial organizational patterns of commercial services and tourist attractions in historic
areas can be classified into five types: fully encircled clustering, semi-surrounding clustering,
overlapping clustering, contiguous clustering, and separate clustering. Based on this classifica-
tion, historic and cultural areas can be classified into an additional three types: commercial
service oriented areas, tourist attraction oriented areas, and commerce–tourism complexes.
High-income commercial development, a high level of vitality, and appealing tourist attraction
construction have different degrees of spatial influence on Chinese historic and cultural areas.
The characteristics of population agglomeration and the spatial distribution of POIs are relevant
here. The categories of POIs in public gathering spaces are diverse, presenting a trend which
entails combining a large quantity of certain POIs with a small amount of other specific POIs in a
spatial distribution. Among these, catering service, shopping service, and living service POIs
account for 80% of the total, and the proportions of leisure service POIs, accommodation service
POIs, and tourist attraction POIs make up the remaining 20%.
(2) Concerning the probability of commercial businesses continuing to attract people when
there are no tourist attractions with regional features.
The cultural aspects of historic areas are no longer the only source of tourist attraction. Along
with development, commercial services have become a source of tourist attraction in historic areas.
In most historic and cultural blocks or their surrounding areas, high crowd concentrations mainly
occur in business circles, transportation hubs, office buildings, and scenic spots. In this study, we
found there were no significant changes in the spatial distribution of the crowds during weekdays,
weekends, or holidays, which illustrated that the business sector has an enduring appeal. Further-
more, shopping services were dominant in historic blocks because local residents make a living
selling to and profiting from tourists; the associated commerce can also help reduce resistance
toward historic district renewal, and can achieve an overall favorable situation among the govern-
ment, merchants, and local residents. Furthermore, sustainable arrangement of the spatial order can
help maintain the vitality of these areas. At present, many historical and cultural attributes of
historic areas have not been fully developed in many aspects, and the form of cultural expression is
not attractive enough to meet the needs of tourists. As a result, many tourists do not have a deep
understanding of the cultural importance of such places and are more likely to be attracted by the
newly developed and prosperous businesses (such as food, souvenirs, and other related shops).
(3) Concerning vitality continuation or over-commercialization, and how to balance the
vitality maintenance and commercial development of historic areas during the process
of tourism development.
First, in the face of the commercial development of historic areas, commercial services and
tourist attractions mutually reinforce each other. Commercial development is the basis for the
renewal of historic areas, because it fully addresses the daily needs of tourists and residents, and
defines their behavior and values with respect to historic areas. Thus, the activity of different
groups is a dynamic regulator for the continuation of vitality. In addition, living service facilities
still dominate historic areas – in terms of both the quantity of facilities and the proportion of spatial
distribution – as they are very important business types for historic areas, since serving local

Abstract
In recent years, with rapid urbanization and development of tourism, historic and cultural areas
have become characterized by strong vitality. However, a dilemma has arisen concerning their
over-commercialization. In this study, 17 Chinese historic and cultural areas, and their sur-
roundings within a radius of 1.5 km, were selected for research. Then, the spatial structure and
population agglomeration associated with points of interest (POIs), including commercial service
POIs and tourist attraction POIs, were analyzed, resulting in five principal findings. (1) In China,
commercial services in historic and cultural areas have become an integral part of tourist
attractions. (2) The relationships between the spatial structures of commercial service POIs and
tourist attraction POIs can be classified into five types: fully encircled clustering, semi-surrounding

should be borne in mind that not all historic areas can be developed into scenic tourist spots.
Finally, the abundance of spatial function and the reasonable collocation of POI proportion will
help promote crowd gathering and enhance the vitality of the space. A significant aggregation,
characteristic of tourist attraction POIs, is evident in the Three Lanes and Seven Alleys, Jianghan
Road, and Zhongshan Avenue. However, it is not evident in other historic areas, as the land use
around this type of area is relatively intensive, and the comprehensive development function is
well planned. However, the tourism quality of the historic areas needs to be improved to enhance
their attractiveness. The commercial service facilities in historic areas and the space configuration
of core areas should be planned together, and arranged based on the status quo. The spatial
planning of the historic area emphasizes its protection. All these measures will play a crucial role
in restraining over-commercialization. As a function of a nodal design for the street system,
moderate improvements and dispersal of groups of people from points of congestion in more
crowded areas can not only enhance the experiences of visitors, but can also help protect core
areas.
Creating a balance between the functional adaptation of modern commercial society and cul-
tural heritage protection and inheritance has become an enduring problem that needs to be
addressed as a part of the renewal of historic areas in various countries. On one hand, excessive
commercial development can destroy the original cultural atmosphere; while on the other,
excessively limiting development can result in a shortage of regional tourist attractions. The
analysis from this research provides a perspective that can inform the planning for historic and
cultural area protection. However, this study only examined historic areas and their surroundings
within a radius of 1.5 km and used open datasets from the Web as data sources, which were limited
to a macro scale. Future research should analyze the similarities and/or differences in POI com-
position, and the spatial structures of concentric zones around historic areas. In addition, combined
with investigations in the field, future research could also select the residents and tourists them-
selves as the objects of the research, analyze their respective behavior trajectories, and quantify
crowd clustering for a more in-depth analysis of the relationship between residents and tourists.

Introduction
With the rapid development of experiential tourism, historic and cultural areas have become
important destinations for providing tourism experiences, which has improved the vitality of the
host areas. As living records of collective urban memory, historic and cultural areas gradually
develop into the means by which historical features are shaped. They are also a medium for the
creation of a new mode of commercial consumption, resulting from the transition to tourist venues.
Heritage tourism can evoke people’s interest in history and culture, by reintroducing them to their
cultural roots (Ginting and Wahid, 2015; Loulanski and Loulanski, 2011). The goal of the United
Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, as it relates to world heritage con-
servation, is to encourage visitation, and to promote historic, cultural, and artistic values (Su and
Wall, 2011). Tourism development can be a mixed blessing, however. As living urban spaces,
historic and cultural areas cannot be subjected to museum-style isolated protection. Tourism can
introduce cultural and historical information to the public in a vivid manner, can enrich the
connotation and extension of culture, and is conducive to the identification, conservation, and
inheritance of cultural heritage (Saarinen, 2010; Yang et al., 2010). In addition, the development of
tourism can encourage new types of businesses, to enrich areas’ attractiveness, and to encourage
sustainable renewal and development. Moreover, as a result of tourism development, destinations
gradually become important social and economic centers (Franklin, 2004). However, over-
commercialization in historic areas can lead to economic, sociocultural, and spatial changes in
local communities (Jimura, 2011; Vural-Arslan, 2015). This can not only affect land use and
people’s daily lives, but can also easily result in the development of a bottleneck of commercial

area, while a buffer that is too small may not accurately represent its surroundings (Gunn et al.,
2017). Walking is more likely to occur within a 1.5-km space, which could be used as a design
parameter for urban planning (Wang and Du, 2015; Wang et al., 2018b), so the surroundings of
historic areas, out to a radius of at least 1.5 km Euclidean distance (approximately 20 min
walking distance) were set as the limits of the research scope (Figure 1).
Research methods
In this study, kernel density estimation was used to analyze the spatial arrangement and distri-
bution characteristics of different commerce and tourist attractions, and then the kernel density
distributions and the Baidu heat maps were overlain.
(1) Kernel density estimation was applied to the spatial distribution of POI data, as a non-
parametric technique. Point features were transformed into smooth areal features, through
quantity calculation, and then the spatial distribution trends of the point features were
analyzed. Visual representations of the point feature density in space were then developed,
using ArcGIS 10.2. It was noted that kernel density value gradually decreased further from
the center of the agglomeration, highlighting the distance attenuation effect of point
features (Okabe et al., 2009; Yu and Ai, 2015). The specific calculation formula was as
follows:

Discussion
On the whole, it was apparent that protection policies had minimized the exploitation of the
historic and cultural blocks, as there were few commercial service POIs in historic core areas,
which demonstrated that the historic areas in the list were well preserved, with limited commerce.
This, in turn, led to the development of an isolation zone separated from relatively rapid urbani-
zation and commercialization, while urban revitalization achieved the extension of the cultural
context and inheritance, in the areas surrounding the historic blocks, exemplified by attractions
such as the First Automobile Works area and Sunwenxi Street. There were, however, many
shopping and catering services located around the commercial service oriented historic areas.
Shopping and catering had become profitable, while living services also provided products needed
by local residents. The tendency towards over-commercialization should be prevented in these
kinds of historic areas. In addition, historic areas with a high reputation for having a low level of
commercial development – such as the Imperial City and the Dashilar Area – were well protected.
Living services, which provide local residents with products used in daily life over the long term,
have become one of the important forms of commercial development in historic areas. This was
because most historic areas in China have traditionally been commercial centers or residential areas,
with reliable locality and authenticity characteristics, leading to domination here by a combination of
commercial and residential functions. In addition, with tourism development and a scarcity of urban
land resources, the functions of historic areas have been transformed into a commercial and resi-
dential composite mix, while a few areas have business-oriented features, such as the Dashilar Area,
or lifestyle-oriented features, such as the First Automobile Works. By providing adequate living
facilities and improving service quality, tourist attraction oriented historic areas have aimed to
provide tourists and residents with a unique and high-quality tourism and leisure experience.
Living, shopping, and catering services are extremely attractive, while tourist attractions,
accommodation services, and leisure services often cause crowds to gather, because accommodation
services and tourist attractions provide priority items for tourists, as well as leisure services to tourists
and local residents. The functional characteristics of these areas cause crowds to stay longer. In
addition, relative to catering and shopping services, the overall numbers of tourist attractions,
accommodation services, and leisure services are so small that people are willing to access these
scarce resources, which demonstrates the preferences and choices of people in terms of resources
relative to space.

Tourist attraction oriented historic and cultural areas
Tourist attraction oriented historic and cultural areas had the following characteristics: (1) there
were abundant tourism resources near these areas, with apparent local characteristics and most of
the tourist attraction POIs and commercial service POIs showed as multiple-core group aggre-
gations. The spatial arrangement of the tourist attractions was homogeneous and commercial
services were mainly distributed on the edge of those historic blocks that were located further away
from the core area. (2) Tourist attractions and living services comprised the dominant spatial
functions in the study areas.
Commerce–tourism complex historic and cultural areas
Commerce–tourism complex historic areas have been found to exhibit the following character-
istics: (1) commercial service POIs and tourist attraction POIs showed a structural form of spatial
dislocation and aggregation, respectively, but a convergence trend was found to exist between the
two. (2) The dominant spatial function types were rich and varied in commerce–tourism complex
historic areas, similar to living services for local residents and shopping or catering services for
visitors.
Following the aforementioned analysis, in terms of the spatial arrangement of POI
aggregation, it was observed that all types of commercial service POIs and tourist attraction
POIs were preferentially concentrated, in either commercial service oriented or tourist
attraction oriented historic areas. As for commerce–tourism complex blocks, POIs covered
almost the entire area and had a relatively even distribution. Notably, the living service POIs
were superior in quantity and spatial distribution proportion whether in the historic or asso-
ciated surrounding areas.

In terms of research methods, in recent years, point of interest (POI) data and heat maps have
been used to show the spatial distribution of crowds and commercial space. Heat maps, based on
mobile location services, have been used to explain urban form and visitors’ behavioral pre-
ferences (Shoval, 2008). Baidu heat map is a function attached to the mobile application “Baidu
map,” which offers colored visual displays of urban population densities. The original purpose of
the application was to help people avoid busy scenic areas while travelling. However the gross data
shown has unintentionally become an excellent tool for research on the temporal and spatial
distribution of urban populations (Wu and Ye, 2016). Baidu heat map data is based on the location
of real-time information collection from the Baidu mobile app. While its coverage is not a com-
plete sampling of the data – and so it is unable to reflect the actual number of people in its data
blocks – the data are gathered from over two hundred million users, which nonetheless makes it
quite effective when indicating the level of urban population aggregation (Ye et al., 2017). It
should be noted that there will be a degree of inaccuracy whenever big data replaces actual
population distribution data (Kang et al., 2012). Wang et al. (2018a) used POI data to cluster grid
cells of a city according to their main function, which served as a reference for determining the
type of vacation destination. In addition, POIs are inextricably linked to modern recommendation
systems, location-based social networks, transportation studies, tourism systems, and urban
planning. POIs can therefore provide suitable travel recommendations based on visits and
description content, as well as information on the adjustment and innovation of the industry
according to spatial distribution and temporal variation (Mckenzie et al., 2015; Santos et al., 2017).
Research design
To address the research questions, we selected 17 Chinese historic and cultural areas in which to
study the relationship between the continuation of vitality and over-commercialization. Data were
selected from the Baidu heat map and POI data were downloaded using the Python programming
language to support quantitative analysis of spatial clustering, kernel density, and map overlays.
The research focused on the following: (1) the spatial agglomeration and structural characteristics
of commercial service POIs and tourist attraction POIs; (2) the spatial function partitioning of
historic and cultural areas, dominated by different types of commercial POIs; (3) the different
characteristics of crowd clustering during workdays, weekends, and holidays, as well as the
relationship between spatial function and crowds. From these focal points, the authors aimed to
achieve the following: to explain the relationship between commercial services and tourist
attractions in historic and cultural areas, to explore how spatial patterns affected crowd agglom-
eration, and to provide a reference on the dynamic balance between commercial development and
the sustainable conservation of historic and cultural areas.
Study area

Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, and the State Administration of Cultural

area’s environment, and this can have a negative impact on people’s cognition of the change of
cultural heritage (Dai et al., 2017; Jimura, 2011). Therefore, it is important to understand the
relationship between commercial development and the retention of the integrity of historic areas.
The rapid development of tourism encourages local residents to rebuild the commercial spaces
in historic areas and their surroundings. It has been reported that, for economic reasons, local
residents set aside the emotional attachment they may have for the old streets, and instead prioritize
their functional aspects of the old streets over their sentimental value (Campos et al., 2013; Liu,
2012). The rise in travel and tourism has also led to a sharp rise in the price of commercial shops
around historic areas. Septirina et al. (2016) researched Malioboro Street in Yogyakarta, Indonesia,
and found that the construction of a shopping center contributed to an economic diffusion effect,
which quickly provided commercial vitality and prompted noticeable change in the surrounding
areas. These changes were related to an increase in tourism, introduction of new technology, and
environments that catered towards tourists’ preferences. It has been reported that there is a tightly
coupled relationship, in terms of spatial structural distribution, between different types of com-
merce and tourist attractions, in historic areas (Ismagilova et al., 2015; Seraphin et al., 2018).
Wang et al. (2015) examined the spaces in historic areas, and classified them into cultural, leisure,
and landscape spaces. They proposed eight types of spatial organizational paths to meet tourists’
needs: “culturalization,” “creativity,” “experience,” “humanization,” “leisure,” “refinement,”
“life-orientation,” and “characteristic.” Meanwhile, Dai et al. (2017) divided the commercial
spaces of historic areas into tourism leisure space and community service space, which have an
obvious spatial separation, characterized by outside-in spatial penetration and expansion. The
spatial pattern of historic areas is not only influenced by tourists and local residents (Sotoudeh and
Abdullah, 2013), but is also regulated by the laws of the market economy (Joaquin et al., 2008;
McGrath et al., 2017). It is apparent that the cohesion and extensibility of tourist attractions in
historic areas are closely related to associated commercial services. The spatial distribution and
structural changes in commercial services change with the location, grade, and development
duration of tourist attractions in historical areas (Martı´nez, 2016; Zhang and Wei, 2017).
Inhistoric and cultural areas, the distribution ofcommercialservicesand different spatial structures
have a serious impact on people’s choices, and consequently, on population agglomeration. The
choices of visitors further influence the type, function, and layout of street space (Guedes and Jime´nez,
2015; Kemperman et al., 2009). Therefore, by analyzing the gathering of crowds and spatial distri-
bution patterns, the market accessibility of tourist attractions can be visually examined (Lee and Kim,
2018; Su et al., 2016). Seguı´llina´s and Capella`cervera (2006) conducted a content analysis of Spanish
tour brochures, to research the spatial patterns of Spanish package tourists, in conjunction with the
attractions and type of tourism that they preferred. In terms of spatial distribution, tourist attractions
follow a hierarchical pattern, and commerce is an important factor in tourists’ choices. Through their
research on a religious tourism destination, the Jatinom Village, which is located along the historical
Soka riverbanks, Hidayati et al. (2016) proposed that, based on tourist preferences, this area should
introduce business facilities with access to comfortable, attractive adventure experiences, in order to
consistently attract crowds over the long term. Thus, it is proposed that tourists’ selection of travel
destinations is not only influenced by the culture of historic areas, but that the surrounding commercial
services are also a factor (Durhan and O¨ zgu¨ven, 2013; Li et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2014).
